keyTerms.definition: Read, evaluate, print, repeat; a scratchpad that actually runs.
Later calls reuse earlier variables; the price is state leaking between tasks.
The session namespace persists across calls.

recall.answer: The REPL reads 6 7, evaluates to 42, prints 42, and loops. The agent sends code as text and gets back text.
recall.question: How does the REPL toy work?

recall.answer: Break the sandbox: os.remove on the host works as designed and destroys data. Two tasks sharing one session leak variables across tasks.
recall.question: What breaks the REPL?

keyTerms.definition: A menu with ordering instructions: name, description, parameters.
The model scores each description against the task and picks the best match.
(name, description, parameters, required); call = (name, arguments).

recall.answer: Name multiply, description Multiply two numbers, parameters {a: number, b: number}, required [a, b]. The model reads the menu; the runtime cooks.
recall.question: What is in the toy schema?

recall.answer: Break honesty: a description saying fast on a 30s tool misroutes urgent calls. Overlapping names like search and search_docs confuse selection.
recall.question: What breaks schema selection?

keyTerms.definition: Think, call, observe, repeat until the answer is ready or the budget dies.
s_{t+1} = update(s_t, a_t, o_t); halting at answer or t = B.
Turns run until done into run until done or B steps.

recall.answer: think -> call(multiply, {a:6,b:7}) -> observe(42) -> think -> call(is_prime, {n:42}) -> observe(false) -> answer(42, not prime). Six states, two tools.
recall.question: What is the toy trace?

recall.answer: Break trustworthy observations: attacker-controlled tool text (prompt injection) gets followed. Calling the same failing tool 10 times burns the budget.
recall.question: What breaks the loop?

keyTerms.definition: USB for AI tools: host, client, server; plug the device in once.
Client sends server/discover; version negotiation prevents method-not-found.
stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for remote with standard auth.

recall.answer: One MCP server exposes file-search. Two hosts each create a client and connect. One server, many apps, no duplicate integrations.
recall.question: How does MCP avoid duplicate integrations?

recall.answer: Break the version assumption: a client requiring a missing method gets method not found. A proxy server with different versions breaks the contract.
recall.question: What breaks MCP?

keyTerms.definition: The ID check at the door: is this token valid?
The wristband: may this identity call file_delete?
Authenticate first (cheap), then authorize, on every call.

recall.answer: (1) Is this token valid (authentication)? (2) May this identity call file_delete (authorization)? A valid token with no permission still fails.
recall.question: What two questions does the server ask?

recall.answer: Break secrecy: a token leaked into logs gives every reader the identity. A connect-time-only permission check keeps working after revocation.
recall.question: What breaks auth?

keyTerms.definition: Nothing allowed unless listed; fails closed on forgotten entries.
A playpen with walls: no network, no host filesystem, limited CPU/memory.
(allow set, deny set, resource limits); enforced before and during execution.

recall.answer: Policy: allow [read, write /tmp, network off], deny [all else]. 6*7 runs; os.remove(/data) is denied before execution.
recall.question: How does the toy policy work?

recall.answer: Break completeness: an unfiltered subprocess-with-shell path voids the sandbox. Allowing /tmp writes without resource limits lets the model fill the disk.
recall.question: What breaks the sandbox?

keyTerms.definition: A promise to stop waiting; converts maybe 30s into at most 5s then a handleable error.
Mass above tau collapses to tau; the tail is where the cost lives.
Timeout tau in seconds; assumes the latency distribution is known.

recall.answer: P(0.2s)=0.9, P(2s)=0.09, P(30s)=0.01. Expected wait without timeout: 0.66s, with 0.30 of it from 1% of calls. A 5s timeout cuts the tail.
recall.question: What does the timeout buy in the toy?

recall.answer: Break the distribution: post-deploy p99 at 8s makes a 5s timeout error on 5% of calls. Timing out a non-idempotent write (C09) is dangerous.
recall.question: What breaks timeouts?

keyTerms.definition: A second chance with a pause; backoff lets the failure clear.
All-fail probability p^r; expected tries = 1 + p + p^2 + ...
Randomized waits avoid synchronized retry storms.

recall.answer: Fail probability 0.2, 3 tries. All-fail = 0.2^3 = 0.008. Success rises from 0.80 to 0.992; two extra tries buy 19 points.
recall.question: What do retries buy in the toy?

recall.answer: Break transience: an hour-long outage makes 3 tries waste budget. Retrying a non-idempotent charge (C09) can double-charge.
recall.question: What breaks retries?

keyTerms.definition: A name tag on the request; the server files results by tag.
Exactly-once effect via at-least-once delivery plus server-side dedupe.
Unique per logical operation; the store must be durable.

recall.answer: Charge $50 with key K. Try 1 times out after the server processed it. Try 2 sends the same K; the server sees K and returns the original receipt. One charge, not two.
recall.question: How does the key prevent double-charge?

recall.answer: Break uniqueness: one key reused for all charges returns the first receipt for every charge. A store expiring keys after 1 hour lets the dedupe miss.
recall.question: What breaks idempotency?

keyTerms.definition: A checkpoint with a human; low-risk flows, high-risk waits.
Freeze the action, get signed approval of the exact (tool, args), execute only that.
t(action) in {auto, approve, deny}; assumes the approver understands.

recall.answer: Read: auto. Write to /tmp: auto. Send email: approve. Delete database: approve + second factor. The loop pauses at the gate and resumes on decision.
recall.question: What are the toy approval tiers?

recall.answer: Break understanding: an approver who cannot read the args JSON approves blindly. Splitting one delete into 100 safe writes evades the gate.
recall.question: What breaks approval?

keyTerms.definition: The tool's promise: schema, named errors, latency SLA.
Named failure modes: RATE_LIMIT, TIMEOUT, AUTH.
(result schema, error enum, latency SLA, side-effect class).

recall.answer: {results: [{title, url, snippet}], latency_p99_ms: 800, errors: [RATE_LIMIT, TIMEOUT, AUTH]}. The model plans retries and fallbacks from the contract, not from surprise.
recall.question: What is in the toy output contract?

recall.answer: Break the honor assumption: a silently added error code falls through the caller's switch. A p99 promise regressing to 5s breaks every timeout built on it.
recall.question: What breaks output contracts?

keyTerms.definition: API design for a reader who never sees the code.
Names are UI for the model; read_file beats f(p, m).
Naming, granularity, description quality, errors, examples.

recall.answer: read_file(path) works on the first try; f(p, m) gets misused three times (wrong arg order, wrong mode). The 31-point gap has standard error 0.065.
recall.question: What does the naming toy show?

recall.answer: Break the reading assumption: if the model pattern-matches names only, descriptions are decoration. 50 perfect small tools make a 10,000-token menu.
recall.question: What breaks tool design?
